title: The Simpsons called President Trump in 2000. The same episode says a woman is next, and the market has a name for her
dek: “Bart to the Future” gave Lisa Simpson the Oval Office and a budget crunch inherited from President Trump. Half of the joke came true. The other half now trades on Kalshi at about 10 cents on the dollar, under the name Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
body:
Sixteen years after it first aired, a throwaway line in a widely disliked episode of “The Simpsons” turned out to be half right. In “Bart to the Future,” broadcast on March 19, 2000, Lisa Simpson is president of the United States, and she opens a meeting with her cabinet by saying the country has “inherited quite a budget crunch from President Trump” [4][1]. The Trump half came true in 2016. The other half, that a woman follows him into the Oval Office and spends her first days counting what he left behind, is still open. As of this week the prediction markets price it at roughly 14 cents on the dollar, nearly all of it on one name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez [10][11].

This is the first of three reports. The second looks at the market's board and at Ocasio-Cortez's own timetable; the third asks whether the “budget crunch” line would even be a joke in January 2029. This one is about the prophecy itself: what the episode actually said, how a gag became a legend, and what has to happen for it to come true a second time.

## What the episode actually says

“Bart to the Future” is the 17th episode of the show's 11th season [4]. The setup is a family trip to a reservation casino, where Bart, caught sneaking in, is sat down by a fire and shown a vision of his life 30 years on [5][3]. Adult Bart is a Duff-drinking slob who gets booed off stage at the rare gig he books [1][12]. Adult Lisa is in the White House, where at her first press conference she introduces herself as “America's first straight female president” [1][12].

Then comes the line. In the Oval Office, Lisa tells her aides: “As you know, we've inherited quite a budget crunch from President Trump. How bad is it?” [1]. A balding Secretary Milhouse Van Houten answers with a chart and two words: “We're broke” [1][3]. Her advisers explain that the Trump administration's investments in the nation's children went badly, that a balanced-breakfast program produced a generation of super-criminals, and that midnight basketball taught them to function without sleep [1]. The country, they say, has “borrowed from every country in the world” [1]. One adviser's proposed solution is cyanide pills [5]. Lisa does not get the bookmobile she wanted [5].

Bart saves the day, after a fashion: he sweet-talks the foreign creditors who have come to the White House to collect into giving America more time to pay [5]. Salon's Sonia Saraiya noted in 2016 that this is more or less the fictional Trump's own method, getting lenders to back off while asking for more [5].

Donald Trump does not appear in the episode. By Salon's count in 2016 he had been drawn only once, in a short the show released the summer before, and in 2000 “The Apprentice” was still four years away [5][2]. The joke was not about a politician. Trump in 2000 was a celebrity developer who had flirted with a third-party run, and his name was shorthand for excess. Dan Greaney, the Emmy-winning writer of the episode, told The Hollywood Reporter in March 2016 that the line was “a warning to America,” and that Trump “just seemed like the logical last stop before hitting bottom” [2]. The pitch was accepted, he said, because it fit “the vision of America going insane” [2]. Critics did not love the result. Salon called the episode “truly abysmal,” and most of its other predictions, drained oceans among them, have not come to pass [5].

## How a gag became a prophecy

The line lay dormant for a decade and a half. It resurfaced in March 2016, as Trump was winning Republican primaries, when The Hollywood Reporter tracked Greaney down and outlets from NPR to Fortune ran the clip [3][2]. After the November 2016 election, the Trump half of the joke was simply true.

The budget half got its first workout in December 2020. On Dec. 18 of that year, Parker Molloy, then of Media Matters, tweeted Lisa's line beside a CNN opinion piece that said Trump was leaving Joe Biden “with a mess” [4]. Snopes checked the quote, confirmed it was real, and pointed out that the CNN piece was about cyberattacks, not the budget [4].

Then came the pearls. At the Jan. 20, 2021 inauguration, Vice President Kamala Harris wore a purple jacket and pearls, the outfit President Lisa wears in the episode, and fans decided the show had predicted her too [6]. CBS News reported that fans read the episode as foretelling that a woman would become one of the most powerful leaders in the country after Trump's term [6]. It took three and a half years to test the theory and one night to break it. When Harris lost in November 2024, Looper observed that the matching outfit had not been enough, and that Lisa's line about inheriting a mess from Trump never fit Harris anyway, since she would have followed Biden [7].

That failure matters for what comes next. The episode's Lisa does not follow a president who followed Trump. She follows Trump. The only way the line is delivered as written is if the person who takes the oath on Jan. 20, 2029 is a woman.

## The fine print

Read as a forecast rather than a joke, the episode makes a short list of claims, and they can be checked.

- **A woman wins in 2028.** Trump cannot be elected to a third term, so the successor the episode describes is whoever wins the next election. The market prices the Democrats at about 66 cents to win the presidency and every woman on the board at about 14 cents combined [10][11].
- **She inherits a budget crunch.** This is the easy one. The federal deficit for the year that ended Sept. 30 was $1.99 trillion, interest on the debt passed $1 trillion, and the gross debt passed $40 trillion in August. The third report in this package goes through the numbers.
- **The country has borrowed from everyone.** The episode's creditors come to the White House in person [5]. Real ones hold Treasury securities and do not need to.
- **She is roughly Lisa's age.** The vision is set 30 years after 2000, and Looper puts President Simpson's term in 2030 [3][7]. Lisa is 8 in the show, which makes the president about 38. Ocasio-Cortez, born in October 1989, would be 39 on inauguration day.
- **Her cabinet includes a childhood friend.** No market exists for this. Milhouse was Secretary of something; the episode never says what [1].

Nothing requires a saxophone.

## The market's name

Here is where the odds stood on Friday, Nov. 6, three days after the midterms. On Kalshi's “2028 U.S. Presidential Election winner” market, Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia led at 22 percent, up 3 points on the day, followed by Vice President JD Vance at 14 and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 12 [8]. Ocasio-Cortez was fourth at 10 cents, with Gov. Gavin Newsom of California behind her at about 8 [10][11]. On the Democratic nomination market, Ossoff was at 25 percent, Ocasio-Cortez at 14 and Newsom at 12 [9].

Among women, there is Ocasio-Cortez and then a long gap. Harris trades at roughly 3 to 4 cents to win the presidency; no other woman appears in RotoWire's top 15 at all, which means none is above about 1.8 percent [10]. Polymarket's U.S. exchange is a touch warmer on Ocasio-Cortez, at 11 to 12 cents, and its Democratic nomination market has her at 17 [10][11].

So the second half of the Simpsons prophecy, a woman directly after Trump, trades at about 14 percent, and the name attached to it is the congresswoman from the Bronx and Queens. That is the figure The Watch will track. Readers may have seen higher numbers for her. In the snapshots The Watch found this year, neither exchange has had her above the low teens to win the presidency; she was at 8.8 cents on Kalshi in August and 10 in October [14][10]. Her high-water mark was on a different board: in August she briefly led the Democratic nomination market at 18 percent, after hinting at a run on ABC's “This Week” [13].

## What would make the episode wrong

Almost everything, which is the honest reading of a 14-cent contract. The favorite is a man. The next two are men. DeFi Rate's seven-day figures show Ossoff up 11 points this week on the strength of the midterm results while Ocasio-Cortez was flat [11]. Prices this far out are thin and jumpy, and the top-15 tables are compiled from last-traded prices that can be hours old [10].

And the prophecy has failed once already. In 2021 it looked like Harris in pearls; by 2024 it did not. “The Simpsons” threw so much at the wall in “Bart to the Future” that a hit was almost inevitable, as Salon argued at the time, and the show's writers have never claimed otherwise [5]. Greaney's own word for the Trump line was “warning,” not “forecast” [2].

Still, there is something to watch. For the first time, the woman at the top of the board is also a person who has said, on the record, that she would decide after these midterms whether to run, as the second report in this package describes. The midterms are over. The decision is next. The Watch has put the odds on a board at [The Prophecy Watch](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/prophecy/) and will update it daily, with a chart that starts at 10 cents and goes wherever the traders take it.
